title: Resources and Training
text:
The following resources may be helpful for staff and students across research, teaching, professional development, equality, diversity and inclusion (EDI), and training. They include institutional support pages, workshops, staff networks, researcher development opportunities, guidance on good research practices, and external courses relevant to research methods, prognosis research, causal inference, and statistical analysis. The resources also highlight practical support for research dissemination and career development, including information on conferences, professional societies, travel and dissemination funding, and opportunities to engage with wider academic and clinical research communities.


The university offers a lot of internal resources and courses for early career researchers, including PGR students, post-doctoral RA’s and new academic staff.


The FBMH Doctoral Academy is the main source of information for PGRs. There are links to the PGR handbook, details of who to contact for a range of issues, and details of training courses and graduate teaching assistant opportunities. On the support page you can find information about the counselling services, financial support and the Disability Advisory and Support Service (DASS). As well as your supervisory team every PGR has an independent advisor, who you can approach if you need any additional advice or support. If you are unsure who your advisor is then their name will be on your eProg profile. The Division also has three PGR tutors who can also help with any queries. They are David Jenkins, Rainer Hinz and Peter Freeman, and their contact details are here.
Another useful resource for PGRs is the University Code of practice for postgraduate research degrees, which can be found here.
PGRs are expected to engage in at least 10 days of training per year. All PGRs have to complete mandatory training through the Doctoral Academy, including an induction when you start and sessions on preparing for your first year continuation report and research integrity training. Details of these are here. Additional training is available through the Researcher Development team, including workshops on managing your research project, research skills, and career development. The timetable for workshops can be found here.



For post-doctoral research staff the Researcher Development website is the best place to go for information on support and training available, as well as a link to the Research Staff handbook. Research staff are recommended to spend up to 10 days per year on professional and career development opportunities. Researcher Development offer a range of workshops covering communication, leadership and career development.
There is also a separate site for training and support for research fellows here.



All newly appointed lecturers are required to complete the Academic Development Programme as part of their probation. This involves attending a number of workshops on teaching, research, and personal and professional development, and completing a reflective portfolio. You can find more information about the ADP here and details about probation here.
Any staff, including research associates and research fellows, who are involved in the supervision of PGRs are required to complete supervisor training, which is run through the Doctoral Academy and Researcher Development. All supervisors are expected to engage with at least one CPD activity per year. Information about the different sessions can be found here.



Every year each member of staff will have a performance and development review with their line manager. These meetings are an opportunity to discuss career development goals and progress. You should agree with your line manager when this meeting should take place and how it will be documented. There is a template for academics and research staff, as well as other helpful information about how to prepare for your P&DR here.
For staff interested in putting themselves forward for promotion there is a dedicated website with details of the procedure, criteria and application guidance.






Team Research is a programme that aims to increase awareness and application of collaborative team research principles. There is more information on their website, including resources and a training toolkit.



The University has an EDI policy that sets out their commitment to promoting equality and providing an environment where all members of our community are treated with respect and dignity. The policy can be found here. Additional useful resources include the Equality Impact Assessments Templates & Guidance and how to get involved with staff networks.







The UKRI Good Research Practice Policies and Guidance has policies that cover research excellence and integrity, ethical research, partnerships, risk and resilience, and openness and transparency.
The Royal Statistical Society offer a range of training resources, that can be found here.
The University of Bristol also offers a range of courses, including causal inference and missing data. The timetable for 2026/2027 is here.





The Prognosis Research website by Richard Riley contains lots of useful information relating to prognostic and prediction modelling, including guidance on methods.
Statistical Methods for Risk Prediction & Prognostic Models at the University of Birmingham, led by Kim Snell. Held online over 4 days, usually runs once per year. Next course is July 2026. More information can be found here.





The University library has a lot of useful information to help you get started with a systematic review, including online courses, in-person workshops and one-to-one consultations with a librarian. More info is here.
Statistical Methods for Meta-Analysis of Individual Participant Data course at the University of Birmingham, led by Joie Ensor. Held online over 3 days, usually runs once per year. The next course is in December 2026. Details are here.





Introduction to Causal Inference course at the University of Leeds, led by Peter Tennant. Held in-person for 5 days, usually runs once per year, next course in 2027. More details here.
Causal Inference in Practice course at UCL, led by Karla Diaz-Ordaz. In-person, 3 days, next course in Feb 2027. Course homepage is here.
The Harvard CAUSALab runs an online summer school each year, with a few courses on offer, details here.





Using Simulation Studies to Evaluate Statistical Methods course at UCL, led by Tim Morris. Held online, over 3 days, next course is in June 2026. More info is here.

title: Research Group Culture and Working Environment
text:
Research Group Culture and Working Environment

Communication
Most members of the group mainly use emails and Teams to communicate. We have a Teams space for the group, which is where people can share relevant papers, seminars, training resources or anything else that may be of interest to the group. You can also use this space to ask questions or get advice on any code or data issues you may be struggling with. Please ask Matt, Glen, Dave or Siân to add you to the channel if you have not been added already!
Some members of the group may work and send emails outside of core working hours, however, please do not feel obliged to reply to these emails outside of your usual working hours!
If you are taking any leave then please put an out-of-office message on your Outlook, letting people know you are not available and when you will be back in the office. Although some group members may read and send emails when they are on leave, this is discouraged. Taking time away from your work/studies is important and we encourage you to switch off entirely!


Project and PhD student meetings
If you are a PhD student or post-doc on a project, you will have regular meetings with your supervisors, line manager, and/or other relevant colleagues. The frequency of these meetings will be by mutual agreement.
Where the meeting is about ‘your’ project, you are expected to prepare and share an agenda before the meeting (at least 24 hours in advance) and circulate brief minutes and actions after the meeting (within 3 working days). If you wish to cancel a meeting, please give as much notice as possible, so that colleagues can reallocate the time slot. A lack of progress is not a good reason to cancel a meeting (it is even more important to meet in this case!); progress includes trying different approaches that fail.
For writing an agenda, a useful template is the ‘3 Ps’:

Progress: what progress has been made since the last meeting?
Problems: what challenges have you encountered? What are your proposed solutions?
Plan: what do you plan to do between now and the next meeting?

Some people like to prepare a slide deck to structure a meeting – this is not essential but can be a nice way to structure the meeting and maximise its productivity.


Feedback
You will often require feedback from other colleagues (or your supervisor/line manager) on work you have prepared. Here are a few useful tips for when you are asking for feedback:

It is useful to clarify what type of feedback you are looking for. E.g., ‘is this in the right direction’ versus detailed in-line feedback on a draft paper. We encourage sharing documents early and often.
Share documents using shared folders in OneDrive/SharePoint, rather than attaching them to emails. This helps with version control, especially when multiple people are commenting and editing.
You should always set a deadline for when you want the feedback returned, including with more senior colleagues. A reasonable deadline is two weeks. Longer deadlines may be required over holiday times and for long documents. If you will need something turned around faster, it is good to prepare people ahead of time for this (e.g., “I will share a draft paper two weeks on Monday and will need the feedback on Friday”).



Use of Generative/Agentic AI tools (e.g., Microsoft CoPilot)
Use of AI in research is a fast-developing and controversial topic. Even within the group, there is a divergence of views on how it should be used. Some general principles:

AI is a supportive tool and should not be used to replace your academic judgement. AI outputs will include a mixture of good and bad, relevant and irrelevant, suggestions. Anything that you share where AI assisted its creation is fully your responsibility and you should verify all contents. This obviously includes cited research!
Places where AI can be particularly helpful include:

Brainstorming and planning o Help debugging and writing code
Checking grammar, and giving suggestions on making text more concise (e.g., to meet a word limit, but obviously check the suggestions)
Summarising a paper (to help decide whether it’s worth reading in detail)

If you are unsure, take advice from a supervisor/line manager/senior colleague. You should also be transparent about when and how AI tools have been used.
Remember that Microsoft Copilot is preferred for use as data placed in Copilot is protected (stays within university file systems). The University is in the process of rolling out Copilot licences to all staff and students.

The University has developed guidelines for staff and students using or developing AI. These can be found in the PGR Code of Practice and the Staff AI Hub. The guidelines include five principles of appropriate AI use which all staff and students are personally responsible for adhering to, as well as guidance on how to apply these principles to teaching and research.


Group meetings and socials
The group meets once a month, usually on the third Thursday at 3pm in the Congregation, Vaughan House. The format of the meeting alternates each month between meetings for the core research group and wider meetings where the invite is extended to other researchers outside of the group with an interest in prediction or causal inference. For the wider group meetings people can volunteer to talk about their research, update about training or conferences they’ve attended or present an interesting journal article for discussion. If you would like to present then there is a sign-up sheet on the Teams space.
Every Tuesday lunchtime we have a catch-up in the ground floor kitchen of Vaughan House, 12:30-1pm. These are very informal and just a chance for us all to catch up over lunch or a brew and get to know one another better!
We also like to hold regular socials, usually following the monthly meetings. Recent activities have included a board games afternoon, a picnic in the park, and pizza! These are not compulsory but we encourage attendance, it is a great way to get to know the rest of the group! Keep an eye out on the Teams channel for details on upcoming socials. If you have any suggestions for activities then please speak to our social secretaries, Molly & Steph.
Alongside research group meetings the division holds quarterly open meetings with (free!) lunch. These are a great opportunity to get updates from the divisional leadership, hear about research going on in other groups and meet other staff and students from across the division. All staff and PGR students working in the division are expected to attend, details are usually sent via the division mailing lists.


Flexible and hybrid working
Most members of the group work regular hours, 9am-5pm Monday-Friday. As stated above, some may work outside of these hours but we do not expect other staff or students to do the same. Some staff do take advantage of UoM’s flexible working policy and work condensed hours, and so may be unavailable on certain days or times of the week.
The majority of the group work in a hybrid manner, with Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays usually the busiest days in the office. We encourage in-person attendance for meetings where possible, whether that’s individual meetings with your line manager or supervisor, or group meetings. We encourage regular attendance in the office – as a rough guide at least two days per week.


Engagement with the group
We try to be a friendly and approachable group and we encourage everyone to engage with the group during their time with us! Not only does this create a fun and supportive working environment for us all, but it also helps establish collaborations and networks, which is an important part of your development as a researcher. If you have suggestions on how we can be more inclusive, or different ideas concerning events, activities or culture, then please raise this at one of our monthly meetings or speak to your supervisor/line manager.

title: Introduction
text: This is the handbook for the Prediction Modelling and Causal Inference research group (aka One Prediction) at the University of Manchester. The aim of the handbook is to provide information for researchers and students working within the group. For more general information about the research group please see the main group website here. The handbook was put together by Siân Bladon and Lana Lai, with input from all group members!

title: Research Dissemination
text:
Here you will find useful information about publishing your findings in peer-reviewed journals, which is an important part of undertaking research. There is also information about attending conferences, which are a great way of disseminating your research and developing your networks with researchers at other institutions.


Please be aware of predatory journals and fake conferences, which may target researchers through unsolicited emails or invitations. These organisations often lack appropriate peer review, editorial oversight, or academic credibility. If you are unsure whether a journal, conference, or training opportunity is legitimate, it is always best to discuss it with your supervisor or a senior colleague before submitting work or making any payments.



There a few important things to consider when preparing to submit an article to a journal.


Choosing which journal to submit your manuscript too can be time-consuming, as there are a number of things to think about. It is important to decide this early on when preparing your article, as journals can vary considerably in the accepted format (e.g. word count, number of tables and figures, abstract structure etc.) and it can be helpful to tailor your writing to the intended audience.
All journals should have their aims and scope stated clearly on their website. Some journals are more focussed on methodology research (e.g. Statistics in Medicine or Diagnostic and Prognostic Research) whilst others are for more clinical or applied research (e.g. International Journal of Clinical Epi, or the British Medical Journal). The JANE tool can be helpful for suggesting appropriate journals, based on either the abstract or keywords. It can also be useful to look at where similar or relevant studies have been published previously, and discuss options with your supervisors or project team.
All journals have a rating, called an impact factor, which is based on the average number of citations published articles receive. Whilst some researchers may target journals with a higher impact factor, we recommend you do not base your decision solely on this. Higher impact journals often have long wait times for initial editorial decisions and the peer-review process, and a high impact factor is not necessarily an indicator of higher quality research.
Once you have decided on which journal you are going to submit to, make sure you read all the information they provide to authors and follow all the instructions they give you. If you do not, then it may cause delays in the submission process if you are asked to correct anything.



Following reporting guidelines improves the transparency and accuracy of research. There are different guidelines to follow depending on the type of study you are doing. The Enhancing the QUAlity and Transparency Of health Research (EQUATOR) network website lists all the guidelines.
Here are a few that are most relevant to this group:

The Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis (TRIPOD+AI) statement should be followed for any study developing or evaluating a prediction model. The checklist and explanation of how it was developed can be found here.
The The Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines should be used for any observational study. More info is here.
The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) should be used for reporting systematic reviews. There is an extension specifically for scoping reviews, which can be found here.
The Transparent Reporting of Studies Emulating a Target Trial (TARGET) guidelines have recently been published here.




If you would like some help with your writing then the academic phrasebank is a great resource. It provides suggestions of phrases and sentence structure for each section of an article or dissertation, for example, how to write critically or report results.
For PGR students the university offers training courses for academic writing, which can be found in the training catalogue. The library also offers a few different workshops for writing and referencing, as well as one-to-one consulations.



Deciding who should be included as an author on an article and the order of the author’s names is important, but can sometimes be a cause for disagreement. It is always a good idea to discuss and agree authorship with your supervisors and collaborators early on in the research process.
The University has Authorship guidelines that cover who should (and should not) be included as an author and what the responsibilities are for authors. These are inline with the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors guidance.
Many journals do have additional guidance on authorship and require the contributions of each author to be stated on a manuscript.



In line with the University’s Position Statement on Open Research and Publications Policy (see the Office for Open Research website), researchers are required to publish articles as Open Access. This means that they are available and distributed without any access fees.
The University has open access agreements with many journals which means articles can be published Open Access at no cost to the author. If you are submitting an article to a journal not covered by an Open Access agreement then there are funds available to cover costs.
There is more information here, about how to access funding, details of Open Access agreements, and how to deposit an accepted manuscript in the Open Access Gateway.



Some researchers choose to make a pre-print of their articles available before it has been published in a peer-reviewed journal. This can be useful for getting research out into the world promptly, as the peer-review process can take a long time. However, there are some drawbacks so it is advisable to speak to your supervisors or project team if this is something you are considering. medRxivis the most common platform to publish pre-prints, or the Open Science Framework (OSF). Some journals do have the option of making a pre-print available through them when you submit your manuscript for peer-review.



All staff and PGR students are expected to set up a Pure profile which contains details of all your qualifications, research interests and research outputs. This will then generate a page for you on the Research Explorer website. For help setting up your PURE profile please see here.
You are also required to set up an Open Research and Contributor ID (ORCID) which is a unique identifier that you can use to keep a record of your research activities throughout your career. For more details, including how to claim your ID, see here.






Here are some conferences that members of the group frequently attend. Attending a conference for the first time can be daunting, if you are unsure about possibly going then please speak to the group - it’s likely other members are planning to attend!

Young Statistician’s Meeting - YSM is a great conference specifically for ECRs. It’s a bit more relaxed than some of the bigger conferences and there are options to present your research through posters or short talks. The 2026 conference is being hosted by the University of Cambridge, more info is here.
Royal Statistical Society International conference - usually held in the UK in September every year. The programme usually contains a lot of medical statistics content, including prediction modelling. There are numerous ways to present your work, through posters or talks, and good networking opportunities! Details of the 2026 conference which is being held in Bournemouth can be found here.
International Society for Clinical Biostatistics conference - ISCB is an annual conference usually held in Europe in late summer (August/September). The 2026 conference will be in Freiburg, Germany. Details are here.
Methods for Evaluating Models, Tests & Biomarkers - MEMTAB is usually held every 2 years, in Europe. The next meeting will be in July 2027, in Utrecht. Details are not available yet, but will probably be posted here.




CHAI Fest 2026


Group members at the CHAI Fest conference held at the Manchester Museum in June 2026. From left to right: Miriam, Alex, Molly, Jamie, Siân, Pedro, Steph and Matt.



Most PGR students will have funding allocated for training and research dissemination. The amount will vary depending on the funder, please speak to your supervisor if you are unsure what your budget is and are unsure how best to use it. For research staff funds may be available through the project grant, speak to your line manager or project PI if you would like to access these.
The Doctoral Academy has a conference support fund for PGR students, more information can be found here.
For post-doctoral research staff the ResDev team also have a dissemination fund. Details of that are here.



The University of Manchester uses the Key Travel platform as its designated travel management system for booking business flights, rail travel, and accommodation. Bookings require prior departmental approval and should not be paid out of pocket unless explicitly authorized. Please contact your supervisor in the first instance on who should be approached.
If you need any assistance with booking conferences or travel, please speak to the divisional operations team who can be contacted at i.pops@manchester.ac.uk. You will need the project codes for the team to charge bookings to, ask your line manager or supervisor for these codes.

The amount will vary depending on the funder, please speak to your supervisor if you are unsure what your budget is and are unsure how best to use it. For research staff funds may be available through the project grant, speak to your line manager or project PI if you would like to access these.
The Doctoral Academy has a conference support fund for PGR students, more information can be found here.
For post-doctoral research staff the ResDev team also have a dissemination fund. Details of that are here.



The University of Manchester uses the Key Travel platform as its designated travel management system for booking business flights, rail travel, and accommodation. Bookings require prior departmental approval and should not be paid out of pocket unless explicitly authorized. Please contact your supervisor in the first instance on who should be approached.
If you need any assistance with booking conferences or travel, please speak to the divisional operations team who can be contacted at i.pops@manchester.ac.uk. You will need the project codes for the team to charge bookings to, ask your line manager or supervisor for these codes.

title: Resources and Training
text:
The university offers a lot of internal resources and courses for early career researchers, including PGR students, post-doctoral RA’s and new academic staff.


The FBMH Doctoral Academy is the main source of information for PGRs. There are links to the PGR handbook, details of who to contact for a range of issues, and details of training courses and graduate teaching assistant opportunities. On the support page you can find information about the counselling services, financial support and the Disability Advisory and Support Service (DASS). As well as your supervisory team every PGR has an independent advisor, who you can approach if you need any additional advice or support. If you are unsure who your advisor is then their name will be on your eProg profile. The Division also has three PGR tutors who can also help with any queries. They are David Jenkins, Rainer Hinz and Peter Freeman, and their contact details are here.
Another useful resource for PGRs is the University Code of practice for postgraduate research degrees, which can be found here.
PGRs are expected to engage in at least 10 days of training per year. All PGRs have to complete mandatory training through the Doctoral Academy, including an induction when you start and sessions on preparing for your first year continuation report and research integrity training. Details of these are here. Additional training is available through the Researcher Development team, including workshops on managing your research project, research skills, and career development. The timetable for workshops can be found here.



For post-doctoral research staff the Researcher Development website is the best place to go for information on support and training available, as well as a link to the Research Staff handbook. Research staff are recommended to spend up to 10 days per year on professional and career development opportunities. Researcher Development offer a range of workshops covering communication, leadership and career development.
There is also a separate site for training and support for research fellows here.



All newly appointed lecturers are required to complete the Academic Development Programme as part of their probation. This involves attending a number of workshops on teaching, research, and personal and professional development, and completing a reflective portfolio. You can find more information about the ADP here and details about probation here.
Any staff, including research associates and research fellows, who are involved in the supervision of PGRs are required to complete supervisor training, which is run through the Doctoral Academy and Researcher Development. All supervisors are expected to engage with at least one CPD activity per year. Information about the different sessions can be found here.



Every year each member of staff will have a performance and development review with their line manager. These meetings are an opportunity to discuss career development goals and progress. You should agree with your line manager when this meeting should take place and how it will be documented. There is a template for academics and research staff, as well as other helpful information about how to prepare for your P&DR here.
For staff interested in putting themselves forward for promotion there is a dedicated website with details of the procedure, criteria and application guidance.

title: Resources and Training
text:
The UKRI Good Research Practice Policies and Guidance has policies that cover research excellence and integrity, ethical research, partnerships, risk and resilience, and openness and transparency.
The Royal Statistical Society offer a range of training resources, that can be found here.
The University of Bristol also offers a range of courses, including causal inference and missing data. The timetable for 2026/2027 is here.





The Prognosis Research website by Richard Riley contains lots of useful information relating to prognostic and prediction modelling, including guidance on methods.
Statistical Methods for Risk Prediction & Prognostic Models at the University of Birmingham, led by Kim Snell. Held online over 4 days, usually runs once per year. Next course is July 2026. More information can be found here.





The University library has a lot of useful information to help you get started with a systematic review, including online courses, in-person workshops and one-to-one consultations with a librarian. More info is here.
Statistical Methods for Meta-Analysis of Individual Participant Data course at the University of Birmingham, led by Joie Ensor. Held online over 3 days, usually runs once per year. The next course is in December 2026. Details are here.





Introduction to Causal Inference course at the University of Leeds, led by Peter Tennant. Held in-person for 5 days, usually runs once per year, next course in 2027. More details here.
Causal Inference in Practice course at UCL, led by Karla Diaz-Ordaz. In-person, 3 days, next course in Feb 2027. Course homepage is here.
The Harvard CAUSALab runs an online summer school each year, with a few courses on offer, details here.





Using Simulation Studies to Evaluate Statistical Methods course at UCL, led by Tim Morris. Held online, over 3 days, next course is in June 2026. More info is here.





Practical use of multiple imputation to handle missing data in Stata course at UCL, led by Ian White and Angela Wood. More information is here
Understanding and Handling Missing Information in Datasets course at UCL. This course is held hybrid once per year but also has a self-led version that can be started at any time. There are more details here
